content: Life expectancy is a statistical measure that represents the average lifespan of a specific population. It is most commonly used to describe the expected age at death for a given human population, which can be categorized by factors such as nation, current age, or other demographic variables. Life expectancy can also refer to the remaining time an individual is expected to live, which can be calculated for any age or group. The calculation of life expectancy is highly dependent on the criteria used to define the population being studied. In countries with high infant mortality rates, life expectancy at birth is particularly sensitive to the rate of death during the first few years of life. In such cases, alternative measures like life expectancy at age 5 (e5) are often used to exclude the effects of infant mortality and focus on other causes of death. Historically, life expectancy has varied significantly. Before the modern health transition, average life expectancy ranged between 20 and 40 years. This low figure was heavily influenced by high rates of infant and childhood mortality. However, if individuals survived childhood, they often lived into old age. One of the most significant improvements in life expectancy occurred with the introduction of sanitation systems, such as sewers, which greatly reduced the spread of infectious diseases. In the last few centuries, the near elimination of infant mortality in many parts of the world has had a profound statistical impact on life expectancy. In the United States, for example, only 50% of children born in 1900 could expect to reach the age of 50. Today, life expectancy in the U.S. is approximately 77 years. Similarly, in India, life expectancy was around 32 years in the mid-20th century but rose to 64 years by the year 2000. However, in poorer nations, life expectancy remains significantly lower, often due to health-related issues such as HIV/AIDS. For instance, life expectancy in some Sub-Saharan African countries has been severely reduced, with figures as low as 43 years. The dramatic increase in life expectancy over the 20th century is attributed to a combination of factors, including advances in sanitation, nutrition, and public health. Medicine has played a role, but its impact is considered marginal compared to these other factors. The most critical single factor in the increase has been the reduction in infant mortality. However, the greatest improvements have been observed in the wealthiest parts of the world. Life expectancy varies widely across the globe due to differences in public health, medical care, and nutrition. Even within individual countries, disparities exist based on socioeconomic status, gender, and other factors. For example, in the United Kingdom, life expectancy in the wealthiest areas is approximately ten years longer than in the poorest areas. Gender differences in life expectancy also persist, with women generally outliving men by several years in many developed countries. This gap is attributed to factors such as lower rates of tobacco, alcohol, and drug use among women, as well as differences in risk-taking behaviors and occupational hazards. Life expectancy is also influenced by environmental factors, such as exposure to air pollution, and by lifestyle factors, including diet, exercise, and access to healthcare. Occupation plays a role as well, with professionals working in offices generally having higher life expectancies than those in physically demanding or hazardous jobs, such as coal mining. In terms of evolution, the lifespan of different organisms, including humans, is thought to be shaped by natural selection. Organisms that are better defended against predators or environmental threats tend to live longer and pass on genes associated with slower aging and better repair mechanisms. Conversely, in environments where organisms face high mortality risks, natural selection favors traits that prioritize reproduction over longevity. Women generally have higher life expectancies than men, even when maternal mortality is excluded. This is partly due to biological factors, such as the protective effects of menstruation in reducing oxidative stress and the presence of two X chromosomes, which provide a genetic advantage. Behavioral factors, such as lower rates of risky behaviors and substance use among women, also contribute to this difference. People with serious mental illnesses, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression, have significantly lower life expectancies, dying on average 25 years earlier than the general population. This is often due to preventable physical diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and respiratory illnesses, which are more prevalent in this group. Life expectancy is calculated using age-specific death rates within a population. These rates are used to determine the probability of surviving to each subsequent age. The resulting figures provide a summary of the current health status of a population but do not account for future changes in mortality rates. Life expectancy is therefore best understood as a snapshot of current conditions rather than a precise prediction of individual lifespans.
